result.summary: 0 exact, 7 behavioral, 0 stub parts. Logic is ok; approximate or missing: timing, analog, power. Check the 21 items in testOnRealDevice on hardware before trusting it.

notes: arduino-uno: Cycle-counted at 16 MHz on a deterministic virtual clock, so delay()/millis() are exact in virtual time. Peripherals the emulator lacks (e.g. some timer modes, sleep) and the crystal's ±50 ppm drift are not modelled.
battery-pack: Never discharges: the voltage does not drop over time (set the voltage prop to simulate a drained pack).

l298n: Switching is instantaneous (the real L298 needs ~1–2 µs, so PWM above ~25 kHz misbehaves on hardware but not here). PWM on ENA/ENB or IN pins is duty-averaged: the module declares the duty on its outputs and the motor averages its current.
dc-motor: First-order mechanics (inertia + viscous and Coulomb friction) integrated every 1 ms of virtual time; winding inductance (electrical time constant ≈ 1 ms) is ignored.
robot-chassis-2wd: Moved by the 2D physics world (Rapier) in fixed 4 ms steps of virtual time.

arduino-uno: Pins are ideal sources with 25 Ω output resistance. Digital inputs use the datasheet thresholds (low ≤ 0.3·VCC, high ≥ 0.6·VCC) and keep their last level in between. The ADC reads the solved net voltage against a 5 V reference; AREF, noise and input capacitance are ignored.

battery-pack: Thevenin model: open-circuit voltage + internal resistance (alkaline AA 0.15 Ω/cell, NiMH 0.03 Ω/cell, LiPo 0.02 Ω/cell, 9 V block 1.7 Ω), so it sags under motor load. No polarization, temperature or state-of-charge curve.

l298n: Bipolar output stage as piecewise-linear drops: high side 0.9 V + 0.35 Ω, low side 0.8 V + 0.35 Ω, so a motor sees about VS − 1.9 V at 0.2 A and VS − 2.4 V at 1 A (datasheet: 1.8 V typ, 3.2 V max total at 1 A). Flyback diodes on every output.

dc-motor: Linear DC motor: back-EMF = Ke·ω in series with the winding resistance, Ke/Kt/friction derived from the rated voltage, no-load speed, stall and no-load current. Under fast PWM (an L298N output while ENA gets analogWrite) the winding is duty-averaged assuming continuous current: I = (duty·V_on − Ke·ω)/R, so speed ≈ duty × full speed, and the battery supplies duty·I. Real drivers in fast-decay mode with a light load can run faster than that at low duty, and below ~20–30 % duty a real TT motor often does not start under load.

hc-sr04: The target is a single distance: a prop, or from the physics world the nearest hit of 7 rays over ±15° (a 30° cone, roughly what measured beam patterns show for walls and large objects; the datasheet's 15° 'effectual angle' is for small targets). No beam pattern, no soft or angled surfaces that absorb or deflect the sound, no multipath, no noise.

robot-chassis-2wd: Top-down 2D rigid body: each wheel pushes with the motor's surface speed, limited by tyre grip (Coulomb friction); sideways slip is resisted the same way; the caster adds rolling drag. No suspension, weight transfer, uneven floor or wheel slip on acceleration beyond the grip limit.
arduino-uno: 5 V / 3.3 V rails are stiff sources. Per-pin current above 40 mA is flagged; total-package (200 mA) and regulator limits, VIN and brownout are not simulated.
battery-pack: Warns above the pack's practical current (AA 2 A, NiMH 5 A, LiPo 20 A, 9 V 0.5 A). No capacity (mAh) accounting.
l298n: Motor current is drawn from the 12V terminal, so the battery sags. 78M05 regulator: 5 V when VS ≥ 7 V, else VS − 2 V. No thermal model (the real chip needs its heatsink above ~1 A).
dc-motor: Draws its real current from the driver and the battery (stall ≈ 1.5 A at 6 V), so supply sag and driver overcurrent show up; heating and brush losses are not modelled.
hc-sr04: Constant 15 mA load on VCC; it measures only with VCC ≥ 4.5 V.

testOnRealDevice: uno (arduino-uno): Total current from many pins (200 mA package limit)
uno (arduino-uno): Anything powered from VIN or the 3.3 V pin (50 mA max)
uno (arduino-uno): Analog readings near the input thresholds
uno (arduino-uno): Upload through the bootloader (arduino-cli upload)
battery (battery-pack): Run time with your motors (capacity)
battery (battery-pack): Brown-out of the Arduino when motors start on a shared pack
battery (battery-pack): Never discharge a LiPo below 3.0 V per cell
driver (l298n): Motor speed at low PWM duty (L298N loses torque below ~30 % duty)
driver (l298n): Chip temperature at your motor current
driver (l298n): Whether the motors reset the Arduino when they start (separate supplies, common ground)
left (dc-motor): Whether both motors run at the same speed (calibrate a per-motor PWM trim)
left (dc-motor): Minimum PWM that starts the motor under load
left (dc-motor): Supply brown-out on the Arduino when motors start (use a separate battery for the motors)
sonar (hc-sr04): Readings on soft (fabric), round or angled obstacles
sonar (hc-sr04): Readings closer than 3 cm
sonar (hc-sr04): Two sensors pinging at the same time
sonar (hc-sr04): Ping rate faster than every 60 ms
chassis (robot-chassis-2wd): Straight-line drift (motors differ, add a trim)
chassis (robot-chassis-2wd): Turning radius on your floor
chassis (robot-chassis-2wd): Whether the sensor sees low obstacles below its mount height
Unplug each module while running to see how the firmware copes (or rehearse with inject_fault disconnect / i2c_nack).
global: Time is virtual and deterministic: real oscillators drift and real sensors are noisy (use inject_fault noisy to rehearse).
All grounds are one node and wires have no resistance or inductance; long wires, motor noise and ground bounce are not modelled.
Supply rails are ideal: brownouts when motors start are not simulated; measure the real supply under load.
